verses.text: Now king Solomon loved many foreign women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites;

of the nations concerning which Yahweh said to the children of Israel, “You shall not go among them, neither shall they come among you; for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods.” Solomon joined to these in love.
He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines; and his wives turned away his heart.
When Solomon was old, his wives turned away his heart after other gods; and his heart was not perfect with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father was.
For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
Solomon did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and didn’t go fully after Yahweh, as David his father did.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, on the mountain that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech the abomination of the children of Ammon.
So he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
Yahweh was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned away from Yahweh, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice,
and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods; but he didn’t keep that which Yahweh commanded.

Therefore Yahweh said to Solomon, “Because this is done by you, and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you, and will give it to your servant.
Nevertheless, I will not do it in your days, for David your father’s sake; but I will tear it out of your son’s hand.
However I will not tear away all the kingdom; but I will give one tribe to your son, for David my servant’s sake, and for Jerusalem’s sake which I have chosen.”
Yahweh raised up an adversary to Solomon: Hadad the Edomite. He was one of the king’s offspring  in Edom.
For when David was in Edom, and Joab the captain of the army had gone up to bury the slain, and had struck every male in Edom
(for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom);
Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites of his father’s servants with him, to go into Egypt, when Hadad was still a little child.

They arose out of Midian, and came to Paran; and they took men with them out of Paran, and they came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house, and appointed him food, and gave him land.
Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him as wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s house; and Genubath was in Pharaoh’s house among the sons of Pharaoh.
When Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers, and that Joab the captain of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me depart, that I may go to my own country.”
Then Pharaoh said to him, “But what have you lacked with me, that behold, you seek to go to your own country?” He answered, “Nothing, however only let me depart.”
God raised up an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah.
He gathered men to himself, and became captain over a troop, when David killed them of Zobah. They went to Damascus, and lived there, and reigned in Damascus.
He was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon, besides the mischief of Hadad. He abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria.
Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother’s name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king.
This was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king: Solomon built Millo, and repaired the breach of his father David’s city.
The man Jeroboam was a mighty man of valor; and Solomon saw the young man that he was industrious, and he put him in charge of all the labor of the house of Joseph.
At that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the way; now Ahijah had clad himself with a new garment; and they two were alone in the field.
Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it in twelve pieces.
He said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces; for Yahweh, the God of Israel, says, ‘Behold, I will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to you
(but he shall have one tribe, for my servant David’s sake and for Jerusalem’s sake, the city which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel);

because that they have forsaken me, and have worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon. They have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in my eyes, and to keep my statutes and my ordinances, as David his father did.
“‘However I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand; but I will make him prince all the days of his life, for David my servant’s sake whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes;
but I will take the kingdom out of his son’s hand, and will give it to you, even ten tribes.
To his son will I give one tribe, that David my servant may have a lamp always before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen me to put my name there.
I will take you, and you shall reign according to all that your soul desires, and shall be king over Israel.

It shall be, if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do that which is right in my eyes, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did; that I will be with you, and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and will give Israel to you.
I will afflict the offspring  of David for this, but not forever.’”
Therefore Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam; but Jeroboam arose, and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, aren’t they written in the book of the acts of Solomon?
The time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.
Solomon slept with his fathers, and was buried in his father David’s city; and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: What a dangerous thing it is to take what we want without asking whether we should. Solomon gathered wives like treasures, and each one became a small door by which another faith crept into his heart. The man with everything was about to lose what mattered most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord had warned plainly—not out of spite, but in mercy. He saw what Solomon could not yet see: that a divided heart at home becomes a divided kingdom. Some warnings are written because the Lord loves us too much to be silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A thousand hearts pulling in a thousand directions cannot answer to one voice. It was not the number of women that condemned Solomon, but that he let them turn him away from the God who had made him wise and great.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the wisest hands grow careless when they grow old and tired. Solomon's heart, which had once burned for the Lord, grew cool and wandered. His father David's faithfulness now stood as a silent judgment against his own turning away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ashtoreth and Milcom—foreign gods with foreign names—became the outlets for the longing his own heart had learned to ignore. When we stop listening to the true God, we do not end up emptied; we fill the space with echoes and shadows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Not perfect—that is the verdict. A man who built the temple, who asked for wisdom and received it, who once loved the Lord completely, became a man who did evil in His sight. The fall was real, and the word rings with sorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High places for foreign gods on the very heights overlooking Jerusalem—a mockery of the temple below, built with such care and prayer. When our faith weakens, we do not hide it quietly; we build monuments to our unfaithfulness where the whole city can see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He did it for them, he might have thought—to keep peace at home, to honor their customs. But accommodation to idolatry is not kindness; it is infidelity to the God who had given him everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord was angry—that simple, terrible word. He had appeared to Solomon twice, drawn near in grace, and was now spurned for foreign gods. Even God's patience has an edge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon had heard the command, understood it, accepted it. And then he chose not to keep it. There is no excuse in ignorance, no refuge in confusion—only the plain fact of disobedience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The covenant and statutes were not bargaining chips to be disregarded lightly. When Solomon broke them, the Lord tore the kingdom from him—justice moving swiftly, not from cruelty but from faithfulness to what was promised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even in judgment, the Lord looked back to David and held His hand. Solomon would die as a king, not a beggar; his son would lose what he could not keep. Mercy and justice walked hand in hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One tribe remained—kept for David's sake and for Jerusalem, where the Lord had chosen to put His name. Even in tearing the kingdom apart, He did not abandon His own purpose or His promise to His servant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord raised up Hadad as an adversary—tools in the hand of justice, consequences woven into the story itself. Solomon's sin did not fall into an empty place; it echoed back in his own days.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old war against Edom, waged by David's hand through Joab, had left a survivor—a boy who fled and lived to return. What seemed finished was not; what was hidden waited for the moment to emerge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hadad was small when he fled, young enough to be carried away. But time had a way of turning a refugee into a rival; the years in Egypt hardened him and gave him strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The journey spoke of preparation—Midian to Paran to Egypt, gathering strength and allies along the way. Pharaoh gave him what a king would give to a kinsman: a house, food, land. Even exile becomes a bed of preparation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hadad found favor and married into the royal house of Egypt—a stranger who became family, an exile who found a place. And yet his heart was never fully at rest in Egypt's embrace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Genubath grew up in Pharaoh's palace, weaned and raised among princes. He belonged nowhere—not to Edom, not to Egypt, but to the strange space between his father's old home and his new one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When word came that David had died, something shifted in Hadad's heart. The old king was gone; this might be his moment. Grief is an opening through which ambition often enters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh offered everything—comfort, honor, a home. But Hadad wanted only to go home, even though home wanted nothing to do with him. The heart remembers what the mind has tried to bury.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rezon, like Hadad, was a man with a grievance, a refugee who became a rival. He gathered others like himself—men with nowhere else to go, men burning with resentment. From such men, kingdoms of trouble are built.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Damascus became his throne, seized in the shadow of older wars. Men who flee from one master often find themselves becoming masters in turn, and the cycle turns slowly on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All through Solomon's reign, Rezon and Hadad stood as thorns in his side—not enough to break him openly, but enough to remind him that his peace was fractured. Adversaries multiplied as his faithfulness crumbled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam—industrious, strong, rising through Solomon's own service—began to see the cracks in the kingdom that Solomon was too blind to repair. A man like this will always lift his hand against a falling master.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The building of Millo, the repair of David's city—works that should have been noble but were felt as burdens. Sometimes what the king builds to restore the kingdom becomes, in his people's hearts, the proof of his weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam was mighty in valor and industrious—qualities a king might have recognized as dangerous. Solomon saw only a useful servant, not the rival already growing beneath his eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahijah the prophet met Jeroboam alone in the field, dressed in a new garment—a visible sign that something old was about to be torn apart and made new. The Lord does not hide His purposes from those He means to use.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve pieces, torn by a prophet's hands—each one a tribe, each one a future kingdom. The garment became a map of what would come to pass.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten pieces for Jeroboam—the Lord speaking through His prophet what Solomon's own unfaithfulness had already sealed. The promise was not cruelty but consequence; the kingdom would follow a man whose heart remained turned toward the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One tribe withheld for David's sake—a mercy threaded through judgment. Even in breaking the kingdom in two, the Lord remembered His covenant and held something back for the faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gods are named again—Ashtoreth, Chemosh, Milcom—and with them the specific ways Israel had turned. The Lord does not accuse in generalities but speaks the names of what has been chosen instead of Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's life would be spared—he would reign to the end, prince over what remained. Not total destruction, but the slow humbling of watching a kingdom slip from his fingers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten tribes would go to Jeroboam—the lion's share of the kingdom. A terrible price for Solomon to see his son inherit a shattered throne.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A lamp before the Lord in Jerusalem—the promise kept to David, the name of the Lord established in that chosen city. Even as the kingdom breaks, the Lord's purpose holds firm in the one tribe that remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam was offered what Solomon had squandered—a kingdom, an opportunity, a fresh beginning. The Lord does not destroy and leave ruin; He raises up what He will use next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But there was a condition: if Jeroboam would listen, walk in the Lord's ways, and keep His statutes as David did, then the Lord would build him a sure house. The opportunity came with the old test—would he choose faithfulness this time?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The affliction of David's offspring would not be forever—judgment would come, but mercy was already woven in. Even in the breaking of the kingdom, the Lord's mercy left room for healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon sought Jeroboam's life, but he fled to Egypt as Hadad had—a fugitive until the old king died. Even a king's anger cannot alter what the Lord has already spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The record of Solomon's acts was written elsewhere, but we know the one that mattered most: his turning away. His wisdom, his wealth, his building—all overshadowed by the fact that his heart did not remain perfect with the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty years—a long reign, yet it ended in sorrow and division. The span of a life does not measure whether it was well-lived; only faithfulness does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: even great gifts squandered, even a kingdom of peace shattered by our own hands. Solomon died and was buried beside his father, but he did not rest in what his father had guarded. The Lord calls us still to the faithfulness that alone brings lasting peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
